ai_verification_nov2026: No AI proof for arbitrary connected graphs; Lovász proved ⌊n/2⌋ paths-and-cycles (1968) and Bonamy–Perrett solved graphs with Δ ≤ 5 (2019), leaving general Δ ≥ 6 open
registry_source: Lovász 1968 / Bonamy–Perrett 2019 / ProofAtlas
core_question: Can the edge set of EVERY connected simple graph G on n vertices be partitioned into at most ⌈n / 2⌉ edge-disjoint paths (and ≤ ⌊(n+1)/2⌋ for all graphs)?
formal_expression: G connected simple graph on n vertices  ==>  p(G) = min{k : E(G) = P_1 ⊔ ... ⊔ P_k} ≤ ⌈n / 2⌉
competing_approaches: Lovász (1968) odd-degree pairing theorem (gives ⌊n/2⌋ paths + cycles); Pyber covering bound; Fan (2005) & Bonamy–Perrett (2019) discharging & induction for Δ ≤ 5 and planar graphs (Blanché–Bonamy–Bonichon 2022 solved ALL planar graphs!)
closest_progress_2026: Blanché, Bonamy & Bonichon (2022) triumphantly proved Gallai's conjecture for ALL planar graphs, and Bonamy–Perrett proved it for all graphs with Δ ≤ 5 and odd-degree-free-cycle classes; general dense non-planar graphs with mixed even/odd degrees remain completely open
affected_industries: Optical Fiber Wavelength Routing, Graph Decomposition Algorithms
contrast_axis: Mixed Path-and-Cycle Parity Partitioning vs. Pure Acyclic Path Edge-Decomposition
strategic_quadrant: Q3: Targeted Technical Frontiers (Focused Impact, High Tractability)

name: Hajós's Cycle Decomposition Conjecture for Eulerian Graphs
originator: György Hajós (reported by László Lovász 1968)
ai_verification_nov2026: No AI proof for general Eulerian graphs; proved for planar, projective-planar, Δ ≤ 4, and large dense graphs (Girão–Granet–Kühn–Lo–Osthus), leaving sparse non-planar Eulerian graphs open
registry_source: Lovász 1968 / Granville–Moisiadis / Girão–Granet–Kühn–Lo–Osthus
core_question: Can the edge set of EVERY simple Eulerian (all-even-degree) graph G on n vertices be partitioned into at most ⌊(n - 1) / 2⌋ edge-disjoint cycles?
formal_expression: G simple Eulerian on n vertices  ==>  E(G) = C_1 ⊔ ... ⊔ C_k  with  k ≤ ⌊(n - 1) / 2⌋
competing_approaches: Seymour (1981) planar-graph proof; Fan–Xu projective-planar proof; Girão–Granet–Kühn–Lo–Osthus (2020) linear-factor absorption for dense Eulerian graphs; Bucić–Montgomery (2023) O(n log* n) general decomposition
closest_progress_2026: Proved for all planar and projective-planar graphs, small treewidth/pathwidth graphs, Δ ≤ 4, and sufficiently large dense Eulerian graphs; for arbitrary sparse non-planar Eulerian graphs, even proving an O(n) cycle decomposition bound (without the log* n factor of Bucić–Montgomery 2023) remains open
affected_industries: Network Cycle Protection, Circuit Layout, Graph Algorithms
contrast_axis: Even-Degree Eulerian Parity vs. Sharp Linear-in-n Cycle Partitioning

registry_source: Erdős Problems Database / Conlon–Fox–Sudakov 2014 / Bucić–Montgomery 2023
core_question: Can EVERY n-vertex simple graph G be edge-decomposed into O(n) (conjectured at most ⌊(n - 1)/2⌋ cycles and edges, or c · n for an absolute constant c) edge-disjoint cycles and single edges?
formal_expression: ∀ simple graph G on n vertices:  E(G) = C_1 ⊔ ... ⊔ C_a ⊔ e_1 ⊔ ... ⊔ e_b  with  a + b = O(n)  (current best: O(n log* n))

name: Bollobás–Eldridge–Catlin Graph Packing Conjecture
originator: Béla Bollobás, Stephen E. Eldridge & Paul A. Catlin
ai_verification_nov2026: No AI proof for arbitrary unbounded Δ_1, Δ_2; Csaba–Shokoufandeh–Szemerédi (2003) proved it for large n with bounded Δ_1 (generalizing Hajnal–Szemerédi), while general unbounded degrees remain open
registry_source: Bollobás–Eldridge 1978 / Kierstead–Kostochka Packing Survey / ProofAtlas
core_question: If G_1 and G_2 are two n-vertex simple graphs whose maximum degrees satisfy (Δ(G_1) + 1)(Δ(G_2) + 1) ≤ n + 1, can G_1 and G_2 ALWAYS be packed edge-disjointly into the same n-vertex complete graph K_n?

name: Erdős Matching Conjecture for k-Uniform Hypergraphs
originator: Paul Erdős
ai_verification_nov2026: No AI proof in the tight threshold regime k(s+1) ≤ n < (5/3)sk; Frankl (2013) proved n ≥ (2s+1)k - s and Frankl–Kupavskii (2022) improved to n ≥ (5/3)sk - (2/3)s, leaving the lower window open
registry_source: Erdős 1965 / Frankl–Kupavskii 2022 Breakthrough / ProofAtlas
core_question: For ALL n ≥ k(s + 1), is the maximum number of edges in a k-uniform hypergraph on n vertices containing NO matching of s + 1 pairwise disjoint edges ALWAYS attained by either the clique on k(s+1) - 1 vertices or the s-star of all edges meeting a fixed s-set?
formal_expression: ν(H) ≤ s (k-uniform on n vertices)  ==>  |E(H)| ≤ max( C(k(s+1)-1, k),  C(n, k) - C(n - s, k) )
competing_approaches: Erdős–Ko–Rado shifting (solved s = 1); Frankl (2013, JCTB) & Frankl–Kupavskii (2022, Adv. Math.) concentration/shifting inequalities (solved n ≥ (5/3)sk for large s); Keller–Lifshitz junta method; Kolupaev–Kupavskii fractional matching polytopes
closest_progress_2026: Solved for k = 2 (Erdős–Gallai 1959), k = 3 (Frankl 2017!), s = 1 (Erdős–Ko–Rado 1961), and n ≥ (5/3)sk (Frankl–Kupavskii 2022); the critical transition zone k(s+1) ≤ n < (5/3)sk where clique and star compete directly remains completely open for k ≥ 4
affected_industries: Coding Theory, Distributed Storage Erasure Codes, Extremal Combinatorics
contrast_axis: Clique vs. Star Phase-Transition Boundary in Uniform Hypergraph Matchings
strategic_quadrant: Q3: Targeted Technical Frontiers (Focused Impact, High Tractability)

name: Brouwer's Conjecture on Sums of the k Largest Laplacian Eigenvalues of a Graph
originator: Andries E. Brouwer
ai_verification_nov2026: No AI proof for general k ≥ 3; proved for k = 1, 2 (Haemers–Mohammadian–Tayfeh-Rezaie), trees, split graphs, regular graphs, and random graphs, while general graphs with k ≥ 3 remain open
registry_source: Brouwer–Haemers Spectra of Graphs / HMTR 2010 / ProofAtlas
core_question: For EVERY simple graph G on n vertices with Laplacian eigenvalues μ_1 ≥ μ_2 ≥ ... ≥ μ_n = 0 and EVERY 1 ≤ k ≤ n, does the partial spectral sum satisfy ∑_{i=1}^k μ_i(G) ≤ |E(G)| + C(k + 1, 2)?
formal_expression: ∀ simple graph G, ∀1 ≤ k ≤ n:  ∑_{i=1}^k μ_i(L(G)) ≤ |E(G)| + k(k + 1) / 2
competing_approaches: Haemers–Mohammadian–Tayfeh-Rezaie (2010) proof for k = 2 and trees; Fritscher–Hoppen–Rocha–Trevisan tree-sharpening; Rocha (2020) random-graph & spectral-majorization (Grone–Merris conjugate degree sequence) methods; Cooper–Frieze extremal semidefinite relaxations
closest_progress_2026: Proved for k = 1 (trivial), k = 2 (HMTR 2010), all trees, threshold graphs, split graphs, unicyclic/bicyclic graphs, cographs, regular graphs, and almost all random graphs G(n, p); even k = 3 for general arbitrary graphs remains completely open despite exhaustive verification up to n ≤ 10

name: Brown–Erdős–Sós Conjecture on Sparse 3-Uniform Hypergraphs (f^{(3)}(n; k+3, k) = o(n^2))
originator: William G. Brown, Paul Erdős & Vera T. Sós
ai_verification_nov2026: No AI proof for k ≥ 4; Ruzsa–Szemerédi famously proved k = 3 (the (6,3)-theorem) in 1978, and Conlon–Gishboliner–Levanzov–Shapira / Delcourt–Postle advanced linear-hypergraph variants in 2022–2024, leaving (7, 4) completely open
registry_source: Brown–Erdős–Sós 1973 / Erdős Problems / Delcourt–Postle 2024
core_question: For EVERY integer k ≥ 4 (starting with the iconic (7, 4)-problem: no 7 vertices spanning 4 triples), must EVERY 3-uniform hypergraph on n vertices avoiding k edges on k + 3 vertices have strictly o(n^2) edges?
formal_expression: ∀k ≥ 4:  f^{(3)}(n; k + 3, k) = o(n^2)   (e.g., no 4 triples on ≤ 7 vertices ⇒ |E(H)| = o(n^2) ?)
competing_approaches: Ruzsa–Szemerédi (1978) Szemerédi-regularity triangle-removal proof (solved k = 3); Sárközy–Selkow & Solymosi–Solymosi (2017) (10, 5) / (k+3, k) fractional-exponent bounds; Conlon–Gishboliner–Levanzov–Shapira (2023) & Shangguan–Tamo linear-hypergraph girth bounds; Gowers hypergraph regularity
closest_progress_2026: Even after nearly 50 years since Ruzsa–Szemerédi solved (6, 3) (which implies Roth's 3-AP theorem!), the VERY NEXT case (7, 4) remains wide open — the best upper bound for f^{(3)}(n; 7, 4) is still O(n^2 / (log n)^c) ONLY for linear hypergraphs, while general (7, 4) lacks even an o(n^2) proof!
